common_name: Prairifire Crabapple (Disease-Resistant Purple-Foliage Deep Pink-Red Crabapple)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; Prairifire is one of the most widely planted and disease-resistant flowering crabapples available.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Prairifire bears deep pinkish-red flower buds that open to vivid dark pink-red flowers, one of the most saturated colors in the genus, followed by small, glossy dark red-purple fruit that persists into winter as a food source for birds. New foliage emerges reddish-purple before settling to a bronze-green, adding a further color dimension. It is among the most disease-resistant crabapple cultivars available, showing strong resistance to apple scab, cedar-apple rust, fire blight, and powdery mildew, which has made it a standard recommendation from extension services across the country. Prune in late winter to shape and remove crossing branches.

common_name: Adirondack Crabapple (Narrow Upright Disease-Resistant White Crabapple)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; Adirondack is a narrow, upright crabapple bred at the U.S. National Arboretum, well suited to tighter spaces than spreading cultivars.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Adirondack, bred at the U.S. National Arboretum, bears red buds opening to abundant white flowers on a distinctly narrow, upright, vase-shaped tree, considerably more columnar than most crabapples and well suited to street tree plantings, foundation use, or tighter residential lots where a wide-spreading crabapple wouldn't fit. Small orange-red fruit follows the spring bloom and persists into winter, feeding birds. It shows strong resistance to apple scab, fire blight, and cedar-apple rust, making it a reliably low-maintenance choice. Prune in late winter to remove crossing or damaged branches and maintain the narrow form.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; Louisa is a weeping crabapple with gracefully arching branches, useful as a specimen or focal-point tree.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Louisa bears clear pink flowers along gracefully weeping, cascading branches, creating a soft, fountain-like silhouette very different from the upright or rounded habit of most crabapple cultivars, making it a strong focal-point specimen near a patio or entry. Small yellow fruit follows the spring bloom, of modest interest to birds. It shows good resistance to common crabapple diseases including apple scab, though somewhat less bulletproof than top-tier resistant cultivars like Prairifire or Adirondack. Prune in late winter, if needed, to remove crossing branches and maintain the weeping form, taking care not to disrupt the graceful cascading habit that defines the tree.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; Coralburst is a true dwarf crabapple with double flowers, well suited to small landscapes and courtyard plantings.

directions: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in well-drained soil, watering regularly until established. Coralburst is a true dwarf crabapple, staying compact enough for small residential landscapes and courtyard plantings, bearing an especially heavy flush of fully double, coral-pink flowers each spring that give the tree an almost solid-pink appearance at peak bloom. It sets little to no fruit, since the doubled flower form is largely sterile, meaning less litter to clean up compared to heavy-fruiting crabapple cultivars. Its small mature size and dense, rounded canopy make it a popular choice as a specimen tree or for planting in a large container. Prune in late winter, if needed, to shape and remove crossing branches.
